OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Let $f(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z]$ be a monic non-constant polynomial. Can the set\[\{ z\in \mathbb{C} : \lvert f(z)\rvert \leq 1\}\]be covered by a set of circles the sum of whose radii is $\leq 2$?
#509: [Er61,p.246][Ha74]
analysis | 
polynomials
Cartan proved this is true with $2$ replaced by $2e$, which was improved to $2.59$ by Pommerenke [Po61]. Pommerenke [Po59] proved that $2$ is achievable if the set is connected (see [1046]).
The generalisation of this to higher dimensions was asked by Erdős as Problem 4.23 in [Ha74].

 Here I provide an attempt assisted by ChatGPT Pro 5.5. In the document, the main claim is:
Let $E=\left\{z\in\mathbb{C}: \left|f(z)\right|<1\right\},$ and \(K=\left\{z\in\mathbb{C}: \left|f(z)\right|\le 1\right\}.\) Let \(E_1,\dots,E_m\) be the connected components of \(E\). For each component, set \(K_j=\overline{E_j}.\)
We call a partition of \(\left\{E_1,\dots,E_m\right\}\) an admissible partition. If \(S\) is a block of such a partition, define
\(
K_S:=\bigcup_{E_j\in S} K_j.
\) Let \(n_S\) be the number of roots of \(f\) contained in the components belonging to \(S\), counted with multiplicity, and define the weighted root mean \(c_S=\frac{1}{n_S}\sum_{\alpha\in S} m(\alpha)\alpha.\) Finally define \(r(S)=\sup_{z\in K_S}\left|z-c_S\right|.\)
Claim: There exists an admissible partition \(p\) such that \(\sum_{S\in p} r(S)\le 2.\) Consequently, the disks \(\left\{\overline{D}(c_S,r(S)):S\in p\right\}\) cover \(K\) and have total radii at most \(2\).
ChatGPT Pro 5.5 is not able to find a counterexample in multiple attempts. (Will still need more verification nonetheless) My approach here is to try to incorporate both results from [511] and [1046]. 
Hope this helps.

A partial proof 
claimed by Boon Qing Hong (using Chat GPT-5.5 Pro, 5.6 Sol).
 Summary:
 Here is a result on the problem up to quartic polynomials, mainly generated by ChatGPT. 
- The quadratic case is trivial.
- The cubic case can be solved by bounding the variables.
- The quartic case can be solved by bounding as well, followed by a computer-assisted proof to bound $\mathcal{F}(X, Y, Z).$ (Code is included in PDF)
GPT also suggested an MST approach as a promising approach among several approaches.
